cards.title: OpenAI’s new agent is a shot at Meta — but can it compete with free?
cards.title_cn: OpenAI 的新代理是对 Meta 的一次尝试——但它能与免费代理竞争吗？

fulltext: OpenAI and Meta’s cutesy AI agents are about to fight to the death.

At OpenAI’s annual DevDay conference, the company pulled out all the stops to compete with its rivals — primarily Meta, whose Muse AI agent platform has seen early runaway success. CEO Sam Altman walked onstage to cheers and announced Dots, a “real-deal AI” agent powered by GPT-6 Astra, “inspired by the cool agents that we all watched in movies growing up.” Similar to Muse, Dots aims for disarming cuteness, taking the form of colorful, personalizable blobs with eyes. OpenAI fired shots at Meta by demonstrating Dots’ ability to not just act as helpful assistants but build metaverse-esque virtual worlds. But in one key area, Dots strikingly fails to compete: price.

Muse’s main selling point is making AI agent access free and frictionless. The company offers a free dedicated virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user’s associated data. OpenAI’s Dots, by contrast, is restricted for now to users on its $100/month Pro plan and up. While anyone with a Meta account can get Muse, most of ChatGPT’s 1.2 billion users won’t be able to use Dots.

There’s an obvious reason for this: OpenAI likely can’t afford it. The AI lab is reportedly currently aiming to raise $30 billion in funding at a $1.4 trillion valuation, per Bloomberg, and it’s experienced 70 percent growth since the beginning of its third quarter — nearing $70 billion in annual recurring revenue, Axios reported. Yet despite its staggering financing, its funds aren’t limitless, particularly compared to a tech giant like Meta. In the past year, some users have accused AI labs of passing costs on to customers amid an AI money squeeze. OpenAI in particular is burning through a lot of cash right now — it expects to spend $280 billion by 2030, per the FT — and compute is expensive, while it’s also facing pressure from investors to button up its bottom line ahead of going public.

“Dots are starting out as a premium product — it uses a lot of compute,” Altman said Tuesday during a private press Q&A after his DevDay keynote, adding, “I think it will help us understand and help people understand how expansive and what AI can do. But you should of course expect us to do a mass-market thing for billions of people someday.”

During DevDay, OpenAI took pains to explain why Dots (with singular agents referred to as a “Dot”) are worth the money, positioning it as not just a capable personal assistant but a “chief of staff” or experienced engineer. OpenAI employee Holly Li told the audience using a Dot was “like talking to a second brain.” Altman said that Dots were built for delegating “ambitious pieces of work,” like QA for an unreleased product, website design, team offsite trip planning, portfolio rebalancing, and email campaign creation. “Specialist” Dots, trained for areas like accounting and legal analysis, are supposed to launch soon, and the company is working with Microsoft to integrate them into its Agent 365 platform.
The goal, Altman said, is to go beyond agents that simply book reservations, purchase meals, search calendars, and schedule appointments — classic use cases for consumer-facing tools like Muse.

When asked during the press Q&A how Dots is different from Muse and Instinct, another popular new AI agent, Thibault Sottiaux, OpenAI’s head of core products, said it’s “capable of actually staying on track in very long periods of time.” He added that the multimodality of Dots, which will allow chatting with an agent via text or voice mode and phone call, will feel like “an incredible extension of you.” (The voice demos of Dots didn’t work at DevDay, though, and though OpenAI leaders highlighted the texting-your-agent feature multiple times at the conference, that feature — already supported by Muse and Instinct — is still slated as coming soon.)

Altman said during the Q&A that the long-horizon and knowledge-work tasks were what set Dots apart, adding, “I think this is far beyond anything else available on the market today.” He said that the agents’ help with triaging to-do lists and supporting employees at work would be “difficult for economists to measure right away” but would hopefully make a “huge difference” in how people feel about their jobs.

Framing Dots as a professional tool not only differentiates Dots from Muse, but could help OpenAI gain ground against Anthropic in the enterprise market. Anthropic has focused on — and dominated in — enterprise AI for years, but OpenAI has devoted more resources to the area over the past year. OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar told CNBC that the company’s enterprise business had doubled since July.

OpenAI leads also tried to promote Dots as safer and more secure, particularly compared to Muse. Alexander Embiricos, the company’s Codex product lead, said OpenAI is focused on having the “most trustworthy, safe, and secure assistant,” highlighting that it’s powered by GPT-6 Astra, the company’s “most aligned model.” During the DevDay keynote, executives also presented “OpenAI Private Intelligence,” a data privacy framework that allows businesses to have “stronger controls” over their data, as well as zero data retention policy options, with no data stored on OpenAI servers.

Altman said onstage that OpenAI hopes to “set a new standard for privacy in frontier AI.” The comments come after Muse was recently lambasted for taking over a user’s Facebook Marketplace account and giving out their address to a stranger without the user realizing.

“I think we’re in a different position to Meta in that they don’t have an AI product that has 1.2 billion users,” Glen Coates, OpenAI’s head of app platform, told The Verge in an interview. “Launching something that makes those kinds of mistakes is something that we would try to take the care to avoid. I think we’re trying to be really deliberate with how we let our agents use plug-ins, how we let agents use your identity and sign-in/sign up for things, how we let your agents pay for things.”

The question is whether all that is enough to beat free. ChatGPT rose to prominence not only by being first but also by being free — and easy to use even without signing in. Muse may be able to dominate in the AI agent space for the same reason. The other hurdle for making these AI agents as frictionless as possible is that Meta offers easy integration with the other platforms it owns, such as Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. (Google’s Gemini Spark agent platform has an advantage for the same reason.) Though OpenAI said users would be able to connect Dots to a wide range of external tools, they may not be as seamless as an in-house integration.

For now, OpenAI is hoping that a better product will trump a cheaper one. “We might move a tiny bit slower, but we also know that if people have Dots that go out there and YOLO-buy stuff on Facebook Marketplace, that’s just not something we want to put 1.2 billion users through,” Coates said. “We’re trying to do it right, basically.”

fulltext_cn: OpenAI 和 Meta 可爱的 AI 代理即将展开殊死搏斗。

在 OpenAI 的年度 DevDay 大会上，该公司使出浑身解数与竞争对手竞争——主要是 Meta，其 Muse AI 代理平台已经取得了早期的巨大成功。首席执行官 Sam Altman 走上台欢呼雀跃，并宣布 Dots 是一款由 GPT-6 Astra 提供支持的“真正的人工智能”代理，“其灵感来自于我们在成长过程中在电影中看到的酷炫代理。”与 Muse 类似，Dots 的目标是消除可爱感，采用色彩缤纷、个性化的眼睛斑点的形式。 OpenAI 向 Meta 发起了攻击，展示了 Dots 不仅能够充当有用的助手，还能构建虚拟世界式的虚拟世界。但在一个关键领域，Dots 明显无法竞争：价格。
Muse 的主要卖点是让人工智能代理能够自由、无摩擦地访问。该公司提供免费的专用虚拟机，其中包含代理和用户的相关数据。相比之下，OpenAI 的 Dots 目前仅限其 100 美元/月 Pro 套餐及以上的用户使用。虽然任何拥有 Meta 帐户的人都可以获得 Muse，但 ChatGPT 的 12 亿用户中的大多数将无法使用 Dots。

这有一个明显的原因：OpenAI 可能负担不起。据彭博社报道，该人工智能实验室目前的目标是筹集 300 亿美元资金，估值为 1.4 万亿美元，据 Axios 报道，自第三季度初以来，该实验室实现了 70% 的增长，年度经常性收入接近 700 亿美元。然而，尽管其融资规模惊人，但其资金并非无限，特别是与 Meta 这样的科技巨头相比。去年，一些用户指责人工智能实验室在人工智能资金紧张的情况下将成本转嫁给客户。尤其是 OpenAI 目前正在消耗大量现金——据英国《金融时报》报道，到 2030 年，它预计将花费 2800 亿美元——而且计算成本昂贵，同时它还面临着投资者在上市前压低盈利的压力。
“Dots 最初是一种高端产品，它使用大量计算，”Altman 周二在 DevDay 主题演讲后的私人媒体问答中说道，并补充道，“我认为这将帮助我们理解并帮助人们了解人工智能的范围和功能。但你当然应该期待我们有一天能为数十亿人做一件面向大众市场的事情。”

在 DevDay 期间，OpenAI 煞费苦心地解释了为什么 Dots（单个代理被称为“Dot”）物有所值，将其定位为不仅是一个有能力的个人助理，而且是一个“参谋长”或经验丰富的工程师。 OpenAI 员工 Holly Li 告诉观众，使用 Dot“就像与第二个大脑交谈”。 Altman 表示，Dots 是为了委派“雄心勃勃的工作”而构建的，例如未发布产品的质量检查、网站设计、团队异地旅行计划、投资组合重新平衡和电子邮件营销活动创建。经过会计和法律分析等领域培训的“专家”Dots 预计很快就会推出，该公司正在与微软合作，将其集成到 Agent 365 平台中。
Altman 表示，我们的目标是超越简单的预订、购买餐食、搜索日历和安排预约的代理——Muse 等面向消费者的工具的经典用例。

当在新闻问答中被问及 Dots 与 Muse 和 Instinct 有何不同时，另一款受欢迎的新 AI 代理 OpenAI 核心产品负责人 Thibault Sottiaux 表示，它“能够在很长一段时间内保持在正轨上”。他补充说，Dots 的多模态功能允许通过文本或语音模式以及电话与客服人员聊天，感觉就像“你的不可思议的延伸”。 （不过，Dots 的语音演示在 DevDay 上并没有发挥作用，尽管 OpenAI 领导者在会议上多次强调了向您的代理发送短信的功能，但该功能（已经得到 Muse 和 Instinct 的支持）仍预计很快就会推出。）
Altman 在问答中表示，长期和知识工作任务是 Dots 的与众不同之处，并补充道，“我认为这远远超出了当今市场上的任何其他产品。”他表示，代理人在分类待办事项清单和支持员工工作方面的帮助“经济学家很难立即衡量”，但有望对人们对工作的看法产生“巨大影响”。
Framing Dots 作为一款专业工具，不仅可以将 Dots 与 Muse 区分开来，还可以帮助 OpenAI 在企业市场上战胜 Anthropic。 Anthropic 多年来一直专注于并在企业人工智能领域占据主导地位，但 OpenAI 在过去一年中向该领域投入了更多资源。 OpenAI 首席财务官 Sarah Friar 告诉 CNBC，自 7 月份以来，该公司的企业业务增长了一倍。

OpenAI 的领导者还试图宣传 Dots 更安全，尤其是与 Muse 相比。该公司 Codex 产品负责人 Alexander Embiricos 表示，OpenAI 专注于拥有“最值得信赖、最安全的助手”，并强调它由该公司“最一致的模型”GPT-6 Astra 提供支持。在 DevDay 主题演讲中，高管们还介绍了“OpenAI Private Intelligence”，这是一个数据隐私框架，允许企业对其数据进行“更强的控制”，以及零数据保留策略选项，并且 OpenAI 服务器上不存储任何数据。
Altman 在台上表示，OpenAI 希望“为前沿人工智能领域的隐私制定新标准”。此前，Muse 最近因接管用户的 Facebook Marketplace 帐户并在用户不知情的情况下将其地址泄露给陌生人而受到严厉批评。
OpenAI 应用平台负责人 Glen Coates 在接受 The Verge 采访时表示：“我认为我们与 Meta 的处境不同，他们没有拥有 12 亿用户的人工智能产品。” “推出会犯此类错误的产品是我们会尽力避免的事情。我认为我们正在努力认真考虑如何让我们的代理使用插件，我们如何让代理使用您的身份并登录/注册事物，我们如何让您的代理为事物付费。”

问题是这一切是否足以击败自由。 ChatGPT 的崛起不仅是因为它是第一，而且因为它是免费的，而且即使没有登录也很容易使用。出于同样的原因，Muse 可能能够在人工智能代理领域占据主导地位。让这些人工智能代理尽可能无摩擦的另一个障碍是 Meta 可以轻松地与其拥有的其他平台集成，例如 Facebook、Instagram 和 WhatsApp。 （出于同样的原因，谷歌的 Gemini Spark 代理平台也具有优势。）尽管 OpenAI 表示用户将能够将 Dots 连接到各种外部工具，但它们可能不如内部集成那么无缝。
目前，OpenAI 希望更好的产品能够胜过更便宜的产品。 “我们的进展可能会慢一点，但我们也知道，如果人们使用 Dots 并在 Facebook Marketplace 上购买 YOLO 商品，那我们就不想让 12 亿用户通过这种方式进行购买，”Coates 说。 “基本上，我们正在努力把事情做好。”
更正：ChatGPT Pro 每月费用为 100 美元，而不是 20 美元。

In December 2025, about a month before the U.S. invaded Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, President Trump had a secret meeting with Elon Musk, Time magazine reports. This was roughly seven months after Musk left his role in the Trump administration at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

During this meeting, Trump “spent hours” talking to Musk’s Grok chatbot, including asking how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of their president, a source told Time. Just a few months earlier, in September, Trump began ordering U.S. military strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump alleged were involved in drug trafficking.

People had apparently been turning to Grok asking about the boat strikes and political climate in Venezuela, as The Atlantic reported at the time. So Grok told Trump that Maduro was a “deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall,” Time reported.
When such celebrations indeed happened after the U.S. invaded on January 3, Trump apparently “came away thinking Grok was ingenious,” that source told Time.
So perhaps it should come as no surprise that in June of this year, the Pentagon’s head of AI said that the military used Gov Grok to deploy and strike targets during the Iran War.

While Grok isn’t the only AI model serving the DoD (OpenAI also has an agreement and Anthropic has been in a back-and-forth over how its models can be used for military intelligence and in modern warfare), Grok may become an even bigger favorite under this administration. Earlier this week, the Pentagon announced that Musk and Anduril’s Palmer Luckey have been tapped to co-lead a study about how advanced technology is, and can be, used in battlefields.

OpenAI is again experimenting with how its conversational AI assistant, ChatGPT, can help users as they shop online. On Thursday, the company announced the global launch of two new shopping features, including a way to virtually try on clothing and accessories and a new favoriting function that can help users save products they like for later reference.

The updates arrive at a time when AI assistants are exploring consumer use cases around shopping. OpenAI already had to pivot from one of its earlier ideas in this space, an instant checkout feature that ended up not performing well. More recently, agentic AI startup Instinct began pushing product recommendations to users, but some felt that the proactive recommendations were an overreach, more akin to ads than helpful suggestions.

OpenAI said its new shopping features leverage the newly launched ChatGPT Images 2.5 model, which the company claims produces more natural lighting and richer textures, follows editing instructions more reliably, and reduces image generation latency.

To start, virtual try-on allows ChatGPT users to upload a selfie or a full-body photo in order to visualize how an article of clothing or an accessory might look on them. This option will appear as a new Try On button in ChatGPT’s shopping results. You can also upload an image of an item, like a web screenshot, and ask ChatGPT to try it on for you.

The other new option, Favorites, lets you save products you discover to a Library in the app so you can come back to them later. (These items will be saved alongside your try-on images, the company notes.)
OpenAI said that ChatGPT can help users shop in other ways, too.

For instance, you could describe a style that you’d like to try, then ask it to shop for the pieces needed to complete the look. Or, you could upload photos of celebrities’ outfits and ask it to find the items they’re wearing that are available for purchase.

The latter sees the assistant moving into areas that Pinterest and Google have dominated in recent years as sources for fashion inspiration and discovery that can convert to sales for online retailers.
Whether ChatGPT will become people’s first choice for this type of activity, however, remains to be seen — especially given that Google launched virtual try-on last year.

Now that LLM-generated prose is everywhere, human beings are eager for ways to sniff it out. While early tells like em-dashes and “delve” are long gone, researchers say there are still plenty of telltale habits that AI models fall back on when writing prose.

A new study from the marketing firm Graphite looked at the writing habits of frontier models, sussing out each model’s favorite words and phrases. While old tells like em-dash use have been stamped out, models still fall back on contrast-heavy constructions, with each model version showing its own unique quirks. The biggest surprise is how broad the scope of tells turns out to be. Graphite found 13,000 phrases that were at least twice as common in the AI content as human content — their definition of a “tell.”

“It turns out that Claude models are actually getting closer to the human word distribution over time,” Graphite’s chief AI officer Greg Druck told TechCrunch. “And for the GPT models, it’s getting further away.”

Studying AI-generated writing at scale required a careful study design. Graphite started with a corpus of 10,000 articles published before the release of ChatGPT, serving as the human-generated control group. Then researchers had different AI models rewrite the articles from summaries, hoping to eliminate as much source bias as possible. With matching samples from both humans and each model, they could compare how often certain words and phrases appeared in AI writing, as well as broader patterns in sentence construction.

According to Graphite’s results, Claude Opus 5.5’s biggest tell is the word “dependable,” which pops up 23 times more often than in human samples. While Opus 5.5 now avoids the “it’s not X, it’s Y” sentence construction, it still tends to say something “is more than an X, it’s a Y.”
Above all, Opus loves to tell you why things matter, using the phrase “this matters” 116 times more often than human writing, while “why X matters” occurs 92 times more often.

OpenAI’s Astra has a different set of tip-offs. This model loves to describe “another dimension” of whatever it’s talking about, and tends to hedge claims by saying an action “may provide” or “can provide” a particular benefit. Its biggest tell is what Graphite calls the “corrective framing,” where a topic is defined as “not simply X” or offered as an alternative, “rather than relying on X.” According to graphite’s research, those constructions were more than 100 times more common in Astra-generated prose than in human writing.

Notably, all the frontier labs seem to have responded to the idea that models overuse em-dashes. In Graphite’s samples, Opus 5.5 used the punctuation mark 99% less often than Opus 5. Astra now uses it 88% less than human samples, whereas Gemini 3.1 Pro has almost completely eliminated the em-dash from its writing.

But while individual tells change, Graphite says the overall number is mostly holding steady. “It’s not like the tells are decreasing,” Druck told TechCrunch. “They are managing to remove the most well-known tells, but other ones pop up. And every model version has its own.”

It’s surprising that tells are so persistent, given the labs’ focus on human-like writing styles. In the Opus 5.5 release, Anthropic boasted that the model “communicates more naturally than prior models,” saying early users “found its writing clearer and easier to follow.”
OpenAI made similar claims when releasing the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna, saying users could “expect to see more clarity, less jargon, [and] fewer odd turns of phrase.”
But Druck is skeptical about how much the labs can do to completely eliminate telltale construction or phrases.

“A general hypothesis I have is that the labs are less able to control some of these things than you might expect,” Druck says. “These are giant models with billions of parameters. They have some finite number of tests they can run, and things slip through.”

现在法学硕士生成的散文无处不在，人们渴望找到方法来嗅出它。虽然像破折号和“深入研究”这样的早期讲述方式早已不复存在，但研究人员表示，人工智能模型在撰写散文时仍然依赖很多讲述习惯。
营销公司 Graphite 的一项新研究着眼于前沿模特的写作习惯，找出每个模特最喜欢的单词和短语。虽然像破折号这样的旧说法已经被淘汰，但模型仍然依赖于对比强烈的结构，每个模型版本都显示出自己独特的怪癖。最大的惊喜是讲述的范围有多么广泛。 Graphite 发现了 13,000 个短语，这些短语在人工智能内容中的出现频率至少是人类内容的两倍——他们对“告诉”的定义。
“事实证明，随着时间的推移，Claude 模型实际上越来越接近人类的单词分布，”Graphite 首席人工智能官 Greg Druck 告诉 TechCrunch。 “而对于 GPT 模型来说，它已经越来越远了。”
大规模研究人工智能生成的写作需要仔细的研究设计。 Graphite 从 ChatGPT 发布之前发布的 10,000 篇文章的语料库开始，作为人类生成的对照组。然后研究人员让不同的人工智能模型根据摘要重写文章，希望尽可能消除来源偏见。通过匹配人类和每个模型的样本，他们可以比较某些单词和短语在人工智能写作中出现的频率，以及句子结构中更广泛的模式。
根据 Graphite 的结果，Claude Opus 5.5 最大的亮点是“可靠”这个词，它出现的频率是人类样本的 23 倍。虽然 Opus 5.5 现在避免了“这不是 X，这是 Y”的句子结构，但它仍然倾向于说“这不仅仅是 X，这是 Y”。
最重要的是，Opus 喜欢告诉您为什么事情很重要，“这很重要”这个短语的使用频率比人类书写的频率高 116 倍，而“为什么 X 很重要”的出现频率是人类书写的 92 倍。

OpenAI 的 Astra 有一组不同的提示。这个模型喜欢描述它所谈论的任何事物的“另一个维度”，并且倾向于通过说某个行为“可能提供”或“可以提供”特定的好处来对冲主张。它最大的亮点是 Graphite 所说的“纠正框架”，其中一个主题被定义为“不仅仅是 X”或作为替代方案提供，“而不是依赖 X”。根据 Graphite 的研究，这些结构在 Astra 生成的散文中比在人类写作中常见 100 倍以上。
值得注意的是，所有前沿实验室似乎都对模型过度使用破折号的想法做出了回应。在 Graphite 的样本中，Opus 5.5 使用标点符号的频率比 Opus 5 少 99%。Astra 现在使用标点符号的频率比人类样本少 88%，而 Gemini 3.1 Pro 几乎完全消除了书写中的破折号。
尽管个人表示有所变化，但 Graphite 表示总体数字基本保持稳定。 “这并不是说信息正在减少，”德鲁克告诉 TechCrunch。 “他们设法删除了最知名的内容，但其他内容又出现了。而且每个模型版本都有自己的版本。”
令人惊讶的是，鉴于实验室专注于类人写作风格，讲述如此持久。在 Opus 5.5 版本中，Anthropic 吹嘘该模型“比以前的模型沟通更自然”，并表示早期用户“发现它的文字更清晰、更容易理解”。
OpenAI 在发布 Sol 和 Luna 的 GPT-6 版本时也做出了类似的声明，称用户可以“期望看到更清晰、更少的行话和更少的奇怪短语”。
但德鲁克对实验室能在多大程度上完全消除泄露线索的结构或短语持怀疑态度。
“我的一个普遍假设是，实验室控制其中一些事情的能力比你想象的要低，”德鲁克说。 “这些是具有数十亿个参数的巨型模型。它们可以运行的测试数量有限，但事情却会被忽略。”

Google Messages just took a step closer to supporting a long-desired feature, RCS video calls. While it’s still very much a work in progress, it’s nice to know that it’s something that could come down the road. But before Google even thinks about rolling out such a feature, it will need to iron out a new wrinkle that’s causing trouble with media sent over RCS.

Over on Reddit (1, 2, 3), users are reporting an issue with Google Messages. When RCS is enabled in the app, these users are unable to send media files to other Android phones, such as GIFs, pictures, photomoji, and stickers. It appears that switching to SMS/MMS solves the problem for most of the affected users.
What’s strange is that the reports claim that there is no problem with sending RCS media over to an iPhone that has RCS enabled. The problem only occurs in exchanges between Android devices.

It appears that troubleshooting steps such as restarting the phone, clearing cache, force-stopping the app, resetting the network, and toggling the RCS connection do not fix the problem. However, one user says that the problem went away after clearing their storage. The user adds that they lost the Photomoji tab in the process and can no longer create them.
It’s unclear how widespread the problem is. We have reached out to Google for comment. This article will be updated when new information becomes available.

Airbnb rolled out its new AI-powered search this week as part of its fall update, a significant step for a company that has been slow and deliberate about AI. Co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said in the past that a chatbot-only interface is not fit for travel discovery. With more AI on the way to the Airbnb app, I caught up with Chesky over Zoom to talk about how the company is approaching it, where interfaces are headed, why consumer AI still isn’t working, and what role voice will play.

Chesky hasn’t changed his mind on chatbots. He said they aren’t good for browsing or shopping because they give you a few options at a time, and you have to take multiple turns before reaching a result. But he doesn’t see the current version of Airbnb’s search as the final form either: its interface will evolve over time.

“I think that I’ve believed for a long time that a chatbot isn’t the right interface for e-commerce. I think what you’re seeing today is also not the endgame for e-commerce or for travel or shopping. I think that there’s going to be some interface that is, you know, I don’t want to call it a midpoint, but something between a chatbot and what you see in the first version we shipped,” he said.

Continued Chesky: “You know, a lot of people want some things … to be fast and easy, like ‘Book me a flight, I don’t want to look at it.’ With Airbnb, they enjoy looking at the product. Travel studies show that people actually derive more pleasure in planning and anticipating travel than they do traveling. So you don’t want to take the inspiration and the browsing and the library experience of dreaming away.”

Chesky sees a second problem with chatbots, which is that they are built for one person. He feels that they aren’t a collaborative interface, which matters for a product that people often use with family and friends. Over the next three to six months, the company’s task is to explore interfaces that enable “multiplayer” AI, meaning AI that several people, such as a group planning a trip together, can use at once.

Airbnb isn’t the only one rethinking what an AI interface should look like. As AI tools evolve, new interfaces are also showing up in apps. Startups like Monogram and, more recently, Wabi are experimenting with “generative” interfaces, which are screens an AI builds on-the-fly rather than ones a designer fixed in advance. Chesky thinks people will see a mix of deterministic (pre-designed and predictable) and generative interfaces.

I asked Chesky how Airbnb is preparing for consumer AI agents, which are tools like Instinct and Muse that carry out tasks on a person’s behalf. Agents will need robust software infrastructure on Airbnb’s end, he said, and the company wants to make itself more agent-friendly. In his view, they could be good lead generators.

“I don’t necessarily know if I believe in a world that there’s apps in the future, but I don’t believe in a world where the apps become data layers of a universal simple UI because when you open your iPhone, there is a reason Airbnb’s app is a different design than DoorDash, Shopify, and Amazon. Our interfaces should be adaptive to the utility and the function that we’re doing. We want to make our app more agentic, and we want to build a lot more user interface controls,” he said.

“If I have an agent, but I also want like really great browse functionality, if I want to be able to message the host like an Airbnb, if I want to be able to compare, if I want to be able to verify my identity, if I want to be able to use a map feature, if I want to then be able to add other items, then if I want to stay in the platform, then either the agent has to do a handoff or the agent application would need to build a bit more of, I think, a robust software developer kit to bring the app to you, so to speak.”
Chesky thinks that there were concerns around AI tools cutting companies like Airbnb out of the customer relationship, but he said that chatbots have proven to be good at lead generation.

The Airbnb CEO is also planning for agent-to-agent interactions through the platform. He explained there might be some interactions within the platform and some with agents of other apps. His thesis is that apps have not always been interoperable unless companies struck a business deal. On the other hand, agents are like “apps with faces,” and when they talk to each other, all apps can become interoperable.

“I think of the Airbnb app as one day becoming an agent, you know, where basically the explore tab has an agent, our customer service has an agent, we’re developing another agent in another service area. Probably eventually there’s going to be a macro Airbnb agent. And that will probably be interoperable with MCP [a standard that lets AI agents connect with other software] to other agents,” Chesky noted.

Chesky argues the bigger problem is that the industry lacks a true operating system built for AI. Right now people are building AI apps for iOS, macOS, and Windows that are not “AI operating systems.” He thinks that in an ideal world, AI would be operable at the kernel level — the core of an operating system — and all components like agents would interact with each other. Right now, he said, the race is to be the “quarterback,” or primary AI agent that users go through for everything.

“The problem with that model [of trying to become primary agent] is no one is developing a full operating system software developer kit. I’ll give you an example,” he continued. “ChatGPT, at the beginning of last year, tried to do their little app store. And I told Sam [Altman]: If you want to be an app store like the iPhone, you need to have a software developer kit and an operating system like the App Store. Otherwise, none of our functionality is going to exist. And of course, it didn’t work very well,” Chesky said.

“I’ve used Airbnb on Muse and Instinct,” he went on. “And it doesn’t work very well. I mean, even hotels don’t work that well, but Airbnbs work even worse. So I don’t think we’ve cracked consumer AI. And for consumer AI to be cracked, we have to crack at a lower substrate, and we need to make the agents [into] apps; all apps need to become agents; all must be interoperable; and all must have much richer user interfaces.”

Chesky thinks that there are two misconceptions in Silicon Valley: first, that the interface is going away and people will just talk and type; second, that software will be completely generative. His argument is that a designer can prompt better software than a consumer can.
He also thinks that as long as the iPhone remains dominant and Apple and Google control the major platforms, apps will likely remain a central fixture.

“It’s really up to Apple or Google, or somebody, to build a new platform for us to really make the true shift from apps to agents. Otherwise, we’re going to have apps that have agents inside them, rather than the whole app being a robust agent that’s interoperable with other agents,” he said.

Before we wrapped up, I asked Chesky about voice, which is gaining ground as apps like Wispr Flow, Willow, and Superwhisper, a new wave of note-taking apps, and built-in dictation in AI tools get people talking to their devices more. He thinks people will eventually speak to computers more than they type. Voice, he said, will play a key part for Airbnb in search and customer service, and the company plans to roll out voice agents this fall to help users.

The company has also been seeing big gains from using AI to ship features faster, he volunteered. On a personal level, Chesky said AI has helped him get information faster, freeing him from so many meetings.

“I think AI is reducing communication layers. One of my jobs as CEO is try to get information. And the way I used to get information was having meetings. Now, I can just ask my AI and I don’t need to have as many,” he said.

Airbnb 本周推出了新的人工智能搜索，作为其秋季更新的一部分，这对于一家在人工智能方面进展缓慢且深思熟虑的公司来说是重要的一步。联合创始人兼首席执行官布莱恩·切斯基（Brian Chesky）过去曾表示，纯聊天机器人界面不适合旅行发现。随着越来越多的人工智能出现在 Airbnb 应用程序中，我通过 Zoom 采访了 Chesky，讨论了该公司是如何实现这一目标的、界面的发展方向、为什么消费者人工智能仍然不起作用，以及语音将扮演什么角色。
切斯基并没有改变他对聊天机器人的看法。他说它们不适合浏览或购物，因为它们一次给你几个选择，你必须转多次才能得到结果。但他也不认为 Airbnb 搜索的当前版本是最终形式：其界面将随着时间的推移而演变。
“我认为我长期以来一直认为聊天机器人不是电子商务的正确界面。我认为你今天看到的也不是电子商务、旅行或购物的最终结果。我认为将会有一些界面，你知道，我不想称之为中间点，而是介于聊天机器人和我们发布的第一个版本中所看到的界面之间，”他说。
Chesky 继续说道：“你知道，很多人都希望某些事情……能够快速、简单，比如‘给我订一张航班，我不想看它。’通过 Airbnb，他们喜欢看产品。旅行研究表明，人们实际上在计划和期待旅行时比旅行时获得更多乐趣。所以你不想把梦想中的灵感、浏览和图书馆体验都带走。”
切斯基看到了聊天机器人的第二个问题，那就是它们是为一个人构建的。他认为它们不是协作界面，这对于人们经常与家人和朋友一起使用的产品很重要。在接下来的三到六个月里，该公司的任务是探索支持“多人”人工智能的界面，这意味着多人（例如一起计划旅行的团体）可以同时使用人工智能。
Airbnb 并不是唯一一家重新思考人工智能界面应该是什么样子的公司。随着人工智能工具的发展，新的界面也出现在应用程序中。像 Monogram 和最近的 Wabi 这样的初创公司正在尝试“生成”界面，这些界面是人工智能即时构建的屏幕，而不是设计师提前固定的屏幕。切斯基认为人们会看到确定性（预先设计和可预测）和生成性界面的混合体。
我问 Chesky，Airbnb 如何为消费者人工智能代理做准备，这些代理是像 Instinct 和 Muse 这样代表个人执行任务的工具。他说，代理商需要 Airbnb 端强大的软件基础设施，而该公司希望让自己对代理商更加友好。在他看来，他们可以成为很好的领先者。
“我不一定知道我是否相信未来会有应用程序，但我不相信应用程序会成为通用简单 UI 的数据层，因为当你打开 iPhone 时，Airbnb 的应用程序与 DoorDash、Shopify 和 Amazon 的设计不同，这是有原因的。我们的界面应该适应我们正在做的实用程序和功能。我们希望使我们的应用程序更加代理，我们希望构建更多的用户界面控件，”他说。
“如果我有一个代理，但我也想要真正出色的浏览功能，如果我希望能够像 Airbnb 一样向房东发送消息，如果我希望能够进行比较，如果我希望能够验证我的身份，如果我希望能够使用地图功能，如果我希望能够添加其他项目，那么如果我想留在平台中，那么要么代理必须进行移交，要么代理应用程序需要构建更多的，我认为，一个强大的软件开发工具包可以这么说，将应用程序带给您。”
Chesky 认为，人们担心人工智能工具会将 Airbnb 等公司排除在客户关系之外，但他表示，事实证明，聊天机器人擅长挖掘潜在客户。
Airbnb 首席执行官还计划通过该平台实现代理商与代理商之间的互动。他解释说，平台内可能存在一些交互，也可能与其他应用程序的代理进行一些交互。他的论点是，除非公司达成商业协议，否则应用程序并不总是具有互操作性。另一方面，代理就像“有面孔的应用程序”，当它们相互交谈时，所有应用程序都可以互操作。
“我认为 Airbnb 应用程序有一天会成为一个代理，你知道，基本上探索选项卡有一个代理，我们的客户服务有一个代理，我们正在另一个服务领域开发另一个代理。最终可能会出现一个宏 Airbnb 代理。这可能会与 MCP（一种允许人工智能代理与其他软件连接的标准）与其他代理进行互操作，”Chesky 指出。
切斯基认为，更大的问题是该行业缺乏真正为人工智能构建的操作系统。目前，人们正在为 iOS、macOS 和 Windows 构建人工智能应用程序，而不是“人工智能操作系统”。他认为在理想的世界中，人工智能将在内核级别（操作系统的核心）上运行，并且所有组件（例如代理）都将相互交互。他说，现在的竞争是成为“四分卫”，即用户在处理所有事情时都要经历的主要人工智能代理。

“这种[试图成为主要代理]模式的问题在于，没有人开发完整的操作系统软件开发工具包。我给你举个例子，”他继续说道。 “去年年初，ChatGPT 尝试做他们的小型应用程序商店。我告诉 Sam [Altman]：如果你想成为像 iPhone 一样的应用程序商店，你需要有一个软件开发工具包和一个像 App Store 一样的操作系统。否则，我们的任何功能都不会存在。当然，它运行得不太好，”Chesky 说。

“我在 Muse 和 Instinct 上使用过 Airbnb，”他继续说道。 “而且它的效果不是很好。我的意思是，即使是酒店也不能很好地工作，但 Airbnb 的工作更糟。所以我认为我们还没有破解消费者人工智能。要破解消费者人工智能，我们必须破解较低的基础，我们需要将代理[放入]应用程序中；所有应用程序都需要成为代理；所有应用程序都必须具有互操作性；并且所有应用程序都必须具有更丰富的用户界面。”
切斯基认为，硅谷存在两个误解：第一，界面正在消失，人们只会说话和打字；第二，人们认为界面正在消失，人们只会说话和打字。其次，该软件将是完全生成的。他的论点是，设计师可以比消费者提供更好的软件。
他还认为，只要 iPhone 仍然占据主导地位，并且苹果和谷歌控制着主要平台，应用程序很可能仍然是核心设备。
“这真的取决于苹果或谷歌，或者其他人，为我们建立一个新平台，真正实现从应用程序到代理的真正转变。否则，我们将拥有内部有代理的应用程序，而不是整个应用程序成为一个与其他代理可互操作的强大代理，”他说。
在我们结束之前，我向 Chesky 询问了有关语音的问题，随着 Wispr Flow、Willow 和 Superwhisper 等应用程序、新一波的笔记应用程序以及人工智能工具中的内置听写让人们更多地与设备交谈，语音技术正在得到普及。他认为人们最终与计算机交谈的次数将多于打字的次数。他表示，语音将在 Airbnb 的搜索和客户服务方面发挥关键作用，该公司计划于今年秋天推出语音代理来帮助用户。
他自愿表示，该公司还通过使用人工智能更快地交付功能而获得了巨大收益。在个人层面上，切斯基表示人工智能帮助他更快地获取信息，使他从大量会议中解放出来。
“我认为人工智能正在减少沟通层次。作为首席执行官，我的工作之一就是尝试获取信息。我过去获取信息的方式是召开会议。现在，我可以直接询问我的人工智能，而不再需要那么多，”他说。

fulltext: I’m looking for ideas I can take back to my own work, from verifying agent-written code and securing dependencies to building software that works where internet access is unreliable.
There are more sessions at GitHub Universe than I can fit into two days. To narrow the list, I built my agenda around questions I’m working through right now:
That puts agent memory, evaluations, and permissions high on my list. I’m also making room for JavaScript tooling and building software where internet access is unreliable. Here are my 10 picks.

Most of us use npm, but the truth is that many of us rarely stop to think about the people, permissions, and release processes behind the packages it pulls in. Karen Li and Leo Balter from GitHub will trace those dependencies through the systems that publish and protect them. I’m interested in what npm audit can’t catch, and where package provenance and OpenID Connect fit into the picture.
View the full session description >

GitHub researchers Cooper Nederhood and Alejandro Carderera built a benchmark from sequences of real pull requests and found that accumulated context can hurt performance. We expend a lot of effort deciding what context to give an agent. I want to understand what to not give. They’ll cover how that research informs their work on agent memory, including features still in development.

You’ve written instructions, built and installed skills, and added your MCP servers. It works for you. How do you make that context useful across a team? Christopher Harrison from GitHub will break down what each tool is good for and how to distribute the right context consistently as your setup grows.

“Open a pull request, but do not merge” is a boundary I want enforced in permissions. Putting it in an instructions file feels like an inadequate setup. Nick Taylor from Pomerium will demonstrate an identity-aware proxy that adds per-identity authorization in front of a hosted MCP server without changing the upstream server. I want to see how the rule holds up when an agent actually tries to act.

A model can score well on a benchmark and still disappoint developers using it. Walker Chabbott from GitHub and Julia Kasper from Microsoft will show how Copilot evaluates models in production, including what the team measures and what they stopped measuring. Metrics help us and models make real decisions, so understanding what to measure is more important than ever. This session is a Sandbox Session, so I’m looking forward to working through the question of what makes an evaluation useful.

The test passed so why is the app still broken? Safe to say we’ve all been there. Jeff An from Momentic will explore how agents investigate applications, reproduce unexpected behavior, and distinguish product bugs from broken tests or infrastructure failures. I’m especially interested in the deterministic controls that limit what those agents can do while they investigate.

In the architecture Achin Gupta from Intuit and Divya Mahajan from Amazon will present, deterministic code handles signal collection, topology traversal, correlation, and scoring. The language model narrates the evidence. That’s a clear split of responsibilities, and I want to understand the decisions behind it.

A workflow with access to credentials and the ability to publish a release is an attractive target. Steve Glass and Greg Ose from GitHub will map supply chain attack techniques to GitHub Actions controls, covering the ecosystem, workflow attack surface, and runner infrastructure. I want a clearer picture of where to put defenses in a pipeline I’d trust with a release.

“Your entire JavaScript toolchain” is a bold statement. I’m glad this session includes a real migration. Alexander Lichter from VoidZero will walk through Vite+, an open source CLI for managing the front-end toolchain. Bundling, testing, linting, formatting, runtime management: there’s plenty of configuration in that list. I want to see what Vite+ replaces today, what I’d need to manage separately, and what’s on the roadmap.

Alex Junior Antwi from Braveon AI will share lessons from building CarbonSight for low-connectivity communities in Ghana. There is a long list of concerns when building for less-than-ideal connectivity scenarios, and shouldn’t we all build for our least-connected users? I’m very excited about the offline demo on this one.

I’ll also join Shishir Tewari from Procore for Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills. I’ll bring the skills I’ve built for recurring work; Shishir will bring his experience building skills for a production data engineering team. We’ll explore when a workflow belongs in a reusable skill. If you’re tired of repeating yourself to your coding agent and want to understand what makes a skill useful in both your work and personal projects, come join us.

Want to see what else is happening at Universe? Think about the topics you are prioritizing, then check out the rest of the schedule here and add sessions to your agenda. And if you haven’t registered yet, there’s still time to pick up in-person or virtual passes. I hope to see you there October 28–29!

GitHub Universe 上的会议数量超出了我两天的时间。为了缩小列表范围，我围绕我现在正在解决的问题制定了议程：
这使得特工记忆、评估和权限在我的列表中名列前茅。我还为 JavaScript 工具和构建互联网访问不可靠的软件腾出了空间。这是我的 10 个选择。
我们大多数人都使用 npm，但事实是，我们中的许多人很少停下来思考它所引入的包背后的人员、权限和发布流程。来自 GitHub 的 Karen Li 和 Leo Balter 将通过发布和保护它们的系统来跟踪这些依赖项。我感兴趣的是 npm 审计无法捕获的内容，以及包来源和 OpenID Connect 的适用范围。
查看完整的会话描述>
GitHub 研究人员 Cooper Nederhood 和 Alejandro Carderera 根据真实拉取请求序列构建了一个基准，发现累积的上下文会损害性能。我们花费了大量精力来决定为代理提供什么上下文。我想了解什么是不应该给予的。他们将介绍这项研究如何为他们在智能体记忆方面的工作提供信息，包括仍在开发的功能。
您已经编写了说明、构建并安装了技能，并添加了 MCP 服务器。它适合你。如何使该上下文在整个团队中发挥作用？来自 GitHub 的 Christopher Harrison 将详细介绍每个工具的用途，以及如何随着您的设置的增长一致地分配正确的上下文。
“打开拉取请求，但不合并”是我希望在权限中强制执行的边界。将其放入说明文件感觉设置不充分。来自 Pomerium 的 Nick Taylor 将演示一种身份感知代理，该代理可以在托管的 MCP 服务器前面添加按身份授权，而无需更改上游服务器。我想看看当特工真正尝试采取行动时，该规则如何成立。

一个模型可以在基准测试中得分很高，但仍然让使用它的开发人员感到失望。来自 GitHub 的 Walker Chabbott 和来自 Microsoft 的 Julia Kasper 将展示 Copilot 如何评估生产中的模型，包括团队测量的内容以及他们停止测量的内容。指标帮助我们和模型做出真正的决策，因此了解要衡量的内容比以往任何时候都更加重要。本次会议是沙盒会议，所以我期待着解决评估有用的问题。

cards.title: 何恺明团队新作：看猫片就能学会ARC挑战
fulltext: 用ImageNet训练encoder
教会AI做ARC抽象推理题的，竟然是猫猫？
何恺明团队最新论文提出了NAT-ARC，一套纯视觉的ARC解题方案。
它不靠LLM，用ImageNet上的猫狗花草做预训练，让模型学会「看」，再迁移到抽象格子推理上。
结果，NAT-ARC表现最好的单模型在ARC-1上跑出了63.4%的pass@2分数，集成后达到70.2%。
这是纯视觉方案首次逼近专用LLM系统的水平。
ARC，公认最难的AI视觉智力测验之一，给你几个彩色格子的输入输出示例，让你推断背后隐藏的变换规则，再应用到新格子上。
过去的主流解法清一色把格子翻译成文字或符号，交给LLM推理。
这篇论文偏不，甚至预训练阶段连ARC格子都没用上。
模型看真实世界学来的视觉能力，就水灵灵地迁移到了完全抽象的彩色格子推理上。
ARC全称Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus，由Keras之父François Chollet在2019年提出。
ARC里每道题的格式很统一，一块最大30×30的二维格子，最多10种颜色，题目给2到5组输入输出示例，挑战者需要从示例中推断出隐藏的变换规则，再把这条规则应用到一个全新的输入格子上，预测它的输出。
这些问题听起来像看图找规律的儿童智力题，但ARC对AI来说极难。
一方面，每道题的变化规则都不一样，没有固定模板可背。
还有就是数据量极少，两三个示例就要归纳出抽象规则，并且精确执行。
这种组合让ARC成了测量AI抽象推理能力的标杆。
目前ARC赛道上占据统治地位的几乎全是大语言模型方案，这些方案的共同思路都是把格子翻译成文本或符号序列，交给语言模型处理。
视觉路线后来才开始崛起。
一批研究者走了一条完全不同的路，他们不把格子翻译成文字，改成了用视觉模型直接处理格子图像。
其中最重要的一步来自同一个MIT团队提出的VARC，这个方法把ARC重新定义为条件图生图翻译任务，用19M参数的视觉模型跑到54%。
LoopViT在这个框架上加入循环推理机制，18M参数达到65.8%。
Loop-OWM用视频预训练模型做few-shot，10.6M参数达到68.5%。
这些模型的参数量比LLM方案小了几个数量级，但效果已经开始追平。
但视觉路线依然有一个结构性短板。
LLM之所以能在ARC上越做越好，核心原因之一是它们通过海量语料预训练，积累下了通用能力，模型越大、预训练越充分，在下游任务上的scaling就越明显。
而多数视觉ARC方案的模型从随机初始化开始训练，没有吃到预训练的红利。
在此基础上，NAT-ARC的目标就是给视觉路线补上预训练这一步，试着打通它的scaling瓶颈。
NAT-ARC的核心思路，是在VARC的视觉流程前面插入一步ImageNet MAE预训练。
MAE，Masked Autoencoder，是何恺明在FAIR时期2022年提出的自监督视觉预训练方法。
其训练过程，是把一张图片遮住大部分区域，让模型从剩下的碎片里把原图复原出来。
通过这个任务，模型就可以理解物体的形状、结构和空间关系。
NAT-ARC的做法是把MAE在ImageNet（包含约130万张猫狗花草等自然图像的数据集）上训出来的encoder权重直接拿来初始化视觉编码器，decoder则从随机初始化开始训练。
整个流程分三步。
微调阶段，每道题只有2到5组示范对，模型用这几组示范试图从中“学会”这道题的规则。
有个细节值得注意，NAT-ARC直接用了MAE的公开checkpoint，没有额外花一分钱预训练。
不过，这个checkpoint原本是为更大尺寸的ImageNet图片设计的，而ARC格子只有64×64像素，尺寸差异很大。
为了适配，NAT-ARC丢弃了原始的patch embedding和位置编码，只保留backbone权重，换成2D RoPE作为位置编码。
简单说，NAT-ARC只保留了MAE在ImageNet上学到的视觉特征提取能力，而把与ImageNet图像尺寸绑定的空间感知部分全部丢掉，用更灵活的方式重新学习。
但为什么看猫狗照片学到的东西，能帮到抽象格子推理？
论文用注意力可视化给出了一条线索。
研究人员把三种初始化方式（无预训练、ImageNet MAE预训练和ARC风格格子MAE预训练）的模型放在同一道ARC题前，观察它们在还没开始训练ARC之前的注意力分布。
结果很明显，随机初始化的模型注意力均匀分散，毫无重点；而ImageNet预训练过的模型已经能区分前景和背景，注意力自动聚焦到格子中有意义的图案区域上。
这个模型从来没见过ARC格子，它在ImageNet上学到的「把物体从背景里认出来」的能力，在ARC格子上天然生效了。
研究人员进一步做了任务级拆解。
他们筛出了15道预训练后显著提升的ARC题目，手动标注后发现这些题集中在两类任务上。
其中6道属于match-and-copy，模型需要识别出匹配的对象、颜色或图案，再把对应的结构复制到输出中；
另外6道属于connected-component reasoning，模型需要识别、填充或重新着色空间上连通的区域。
这两类能力恰好对应自然图像里的视觉先验。
在ImageNet上看猫学到的「把猫从草地背景里分出来」，到了ARC里变成了「把这块连通的彩色区域从格子里认出来」。
视觉世界和抽象世界的底层逻辑，在物体分组、图案匹配、区域分割这些操作上，原来共享同一套表征。
NAT-ARC最终在ARC-1上的成绩如下。
表现最好的单模型采用huge尺度，参数量0.6B，pass@2成绩达到63.4±0.7%。
集成时，研究人员把三种不同预训练策略（无预训练、ImageNet MAE预训练、ARC风格格子MAE预训练）分别训出的模型池化在一起做多数投票，拿到70.2±0.6% pass@2，总参数量约2B。
作为参照，专门针对ARC微调的The ARChitects拿到71.6%，用的是8B的语言模型。
视觉路线用四分之一的参数量，打到了专用LLM系统的城下。
数字之外，这篇论文最重要的一个发现，就是预训练打通了视觉路线的scaling瓶颈。
没有预训练时，模型越大效果反而越差；加上预训练后，scaling才开始代理正收益。
先看训练曲线。在离线训练阶段，用了ImageNet预训练的模型收敛速度明显更快，在base、large、huge三个尺度上都是如此，最终精度也更高。
但最有意思的发现藏在scaling曲线里。
没有预训练时，模型从base到large性能还能涨，但从large到huge反而掉点了。
模型变大，效果变差，这在深度学习里不是常见现象，说明ARC这个任务的数据量实在太少，模型容量增长带来的不是更强的泛化而是过拟合。
而加上ImageNet预训练后，scaling曲线变得健康了，base、large、huge三个尺度一路向上，模型越大效果越好。
论文里最酷的一个实验是一个可视化验证。
研究人员训了一个autoencoder，把ImageNet图像映射到一个60×60、10种颜色的离散格子表示上，相当于把一张猫片「翻译」成了ARC格子。
然后，他们用NAT-ARC对这个格子执行ARC变换，旋转180°、加一圈蓝色边框，再解码回像素。
结果，猫确实被转了，边框也确实加上了。这个从猫猫里训练出的模型，又在任务里回到了猫猫之中。
这个实验把「自然图像和ARC格子共享同一套表征空间」从统计数字变成了可视化证据。
在ARC格子上学会的变换规则，可以直接应用到自然图像的潜在表示上，反过来也一样。
抽象规则和视觉表征之间的连接，是这两个世界本来就有的。
论文一作Xiaoman Delores Ding，MIT CSAIL成员，来自何恺明组。
她同时也是VARC的一作，这篇NAT-ARC相当于在自己上一篇工作的基础上继续往前推。
其余作者包括胡珂雅（Keya Hu），是何恺明首批女弟子之一，本科毕业于上海交通大学。
还有Katelyn Gan和Victor Yin，同样来自MIT，两人都是本科生，且均在CSAIL担任student researcher。
通讯作者何恺明不必多说，他是ResNet和MAE的作者，从这两个工作几乎可以串起近十年视觉AI的主线。
他从进入MIT后持续产出视觉基础工作，这篇论文用的正是他自己四年前提出的MAE作为预训练工具，等于用自己的旧武器打通了一条新路。
VARC已被CVPR 2026接收，NAT-ARC是它的直接后续。
这个团队连续两篇论文坚持纯视觉路线解ARC，在LLM大行其道的赛道上，它们正在用实验数据不断突破视觉路线的天花板。
